overview: Burgundian rulers first established a kingdom near the Rhine, then governed a new realm around the western Alps and Rhône after Roman authorities settled survivors in Sapaudia in 443. Their subjects included established Roman provincial communities. This is the fifth- and early sixth-century kingdom, centuries before the famous medieval duchy of Burgundy.

periods.title: Rhine kingdom and catastrophe
periods.summary: A Rhine kingdom emerged in the early fifth century; its army suffered destruction in 436.

periods.title: A Rhône and Alpine kingdom
periods.summary: Settlement in Sapaudia preceded expansion toward Lyon. Frankish kings defeated and partitioned the kingdom by 534.

sections.title: Families, work and the rules of ordinary life

items.text: A Roman-law collection compiled in the Burgundian kingdom borrowed from earlier Roman legislation rather than starting law from scratch. Modern scholarship places it in the early sixth century. Its subjects include inheritance, sales, contracts and guardianship: royal government reached into household affairs.

Its guardianship rules gave a willing mother priority over other prospective guardians. This concerns legal management for children, especially their property. It recognizes a maternal role without establishing equal legal standing for all women.

The collection required a seller to stand by a completed sale. Market exchanges could become courtroom arguments when someone wanted a bargain undone. These rules reveal lawmakers’ intentions, rather than how every village transaction worked.

One provision required compensation when someone deliberately frightened a horse so badly that it died. Denying an offense and then being proved responsible increased the payment. Working animals mattered enough for a very particular dispute to enter a legal handbook.

The courts’ calendar made room for harvesting and grape gathering as well as Christian festivals. Ordinary lawsuits were forbidden during these breaks, although fiscal business had an exception. Even legal paperwork had to reckon with the farming year.

sections.title: What graves and an abbey reveal

items.text: The cemetery at Sézegnin near Geneva contained more than 700 burials spanning the late fourth to eighth centuries. That long sequence crosses the Burgundian kingdom’s rise and conquest. It lets archaeologists investigate communities over generations rather than treating every grave as a separate incoming people.

Regional excavations distinguish earth graves, wooden burial containers and later stone constructions. Changes in materials and arrangement help date funerary practices. A stone-lined grave tells us about burial choices and labor; by itself it does not identify the language spoken by the person buried there.

At Geneva’s Saint-Antoine cemetery, researchers examined people of different ages but found some of the youngest children underrepresented. A separate burial area is one possible explanation. Archaeologists cannot simply count the surviving graves and assume they represent every child born in the community.

Sigismund founded the monastery at Agaune, now Saint-Maurice, in 515. Royal support linked the dynasty to an important Christian shrine. The foundation also created an institution whose daily routines and surviving records outlasted the independent kingdom.

Agaune became known for continual praise, with groups of monks taking turns singing. Think of a choir relay: the aim was continuity of worship, not requiring one exhausted singer to carry on forever. It was a demanding organized routine within this monastery.

The abbey stood on an important Rhône route toward Alpine crossings. Its 515 inauguration is associated with a sermon by Bishop Avitus. Travel, royal ceremony and religious learning met at a specific place, rather than belonging to separate worlds.

sections.title: A few words from their legal world

items.text: The Latin heading “De tutelis minorum” means “On the guardianship of minors.” It appears as title 36 of the Roman-law collection transmitted from the kingdom. This is administrative Latin preserved through manuscript copying, not a reconstructed sentence in the poorly documented Burgundian vernacular.

ending.text: Frankish armies defeated the kingdom in 532, and Frankish rulers divided it in 534. Communities, laws and religious institutions continued after royal independence ended. The map’s 600 endpoint is a coverage boundary, not the date of the conquest.
